paragraphs.heading: What a core is
paragraphs.text: A planetary core is the innermost layer, or layers, of a planet. It can be entirely liquid, or a mix of solid and liquid layers, as in Earth. Across the Solar System, cores range from about 20% of a world's radius in the Moon to 85% in Mercury. Gas giants have cores too, though what they are made of is still debated: stony iron, ice, or fluid metallic hydrogen are all possible.

paragraphs.heading: Studying what cannot be reached
paragraphs.text: No drill can get to a core, and almost no samples are known for certain to come from one. So scientists study cores indirectly, through seismology, mineral physics and planetary dynamics. For other planets, where there are no seismometers on the surface, cores are inferred from calculations based on spacecraft fly-bys, such as NASA's Mariner 10 at Mercury and Venus. A planet's average density and its moment of inertia constrain its structure: a value under 0.4 means its mass is concentrated toward the centre, and Mercury's 0.346 is evidence that it has a core.

paragraphs.heading: Finding Earth's core
paragraphs.text: In 1797 Henry Cavendish worked out that Earth's average density was 5.48 times that of water, which led to the accepted view that the interior was much denser. After iron meteorites were found, Emil Wiechert proposed in 1898 that Earth had a similar make-up, but that its iron had settled toward the middle. Richard Dixon Oldham first detected the core in 1906, when he found the P-wave shadow zone. By 1936 seismologists knew the size of the whole core and where the fluid outer core meets the solid inner core.

paragraphs.heading: How cores form
paragraphs.text: Planets grow from flattened disks of dust and gas that clump, within thousands of years, into bodies around 10 km across, and then over millions of years into full planets. Over time a young planet differentiates, changing from one uniform body into several different parts, and in Earth's case metal separated out into a core beneath the mantle. The hafnium-tungsten isotope system shows that metal in iron meteorites separated in under 5 million years, and that Earth's core formed within 25 million years. Giant collisions mattered too: in the giant impact hypothesis, a hypothetical Mars-sized planet called Theia struck the early Earth, and most of the iron from both ended up in Earth's core.

paragraphs.heading: What Earth's core is made of
paragraphs.text: By combining a chondrite-based reference model with the known make-up of the crust and mantle, researchers estimate the core at 85% iron, 5% nickel, 0.9% chromium and 0.25% cobalt. That leaves a weight shortfall of 5–10% in the outer core and 4–5% in the inner core, put down to lighter elements: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, sulfur, phosphorus and silicon. Sulfur may make up 1.9% of the core by weight and phosphorus up to 0.2%, while hydrogen and carbon add only a little because most of them were lost early on. Silicon and oxygen make up the rest, though how much of each is still argued over.

paragraphs.heading: Cores of other worlds
paragraphs.text: The Moon's inner structure was mapped in 1974 using moonquake data from the Apollo missions. Its core has a radius of 300 km, with a liquid outer layer making up 60% of the core's volume around a solid centre. Gas giant cores are small compared with their planets but can still outweigh Earth: Jupiter's has 10–30 times Earth's mass, and the core of the exoplanet HD 149026 b may weigh as much as 100 Earths.
